nameStory: Train Track Moss earned its name from its habit of growing along railroad tracks, where it thrives in the disturbed, well-drained gravel ballast between the rails. Early botanists noticed how this tough little moss seemed to follow the iron roads across the landscape, carpeting the spaces where trains rumble by.
description: Train Track Moss is a small, creeping moss that forms loose, spreading mats rather than dense cushions. The individual plants are tiny, rarely more than an inch tall, with stems that crawl along surfaces and send up short, upright branches. Its leaves are small and pressed close to the stem when dry, giving it a somewhat flattened appearance that helps it survive in harsh, exposed conditions.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms loose, creeping mats with prostrate main stems and short upright branches, creating a low carpet-like appearance

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny, oval leaves that press tightly against the stem when dry, making the plant look almost scaly, but spread out slightly when moist

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on rock surfaces, concrete, or gravelly areas with good drainage and frequent disturbance

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Dull green when moist, turning grayish-green to brownish when dry, with a somewhat dusty appearance

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels rough and wiry to the touch, much coarser than typical cushion mosses, with a brittle quality when dry

habitat: Train Track Moss prefers disturbed, well-drained surfaces like railroad ballast, roadside gravel, concrete walls, and exposed rock faces throughout New England. It's particularly common along transportation corridors where regular disturbance prevents other plants from taking over. You'll find it from sea level to moderate elevations, always in areas with good air circulation and minimal competition from larger plants.

seasonality.spring: Fresh growth begins as moisture increases, with the grayish winter appearance gradually turning greener. This is the best time to see the contrast between old and new growth.
seasonality.summer: Develops its fullest green color during humid periods, though it can look quite brown and dormant during dry spells. Sporophytes may be present on mature patches.
seasonality.fall: Continues growing actively during cool, moist weather. The moss often looks its healthiest in autumn when summer heat stress ends but before winter dormancy begins.
seasonality.winter: Becomes dormant and takes on a grayish-brown color, but remains visible and identifiable. The creeping growth form becomes most apparent when deciduous vegetation dies back.

funFact: This moss is so tough it can actually grow in the gravel between active railroad tracks, surviving the vibrations, diesel fumes, and crushing weight of freight trains that would kill most other plants!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other small rock-dwelling mosses, but Train Track Moss's distinctly creeping, mat-forming growth sets it apart from the upright cushion-forming species. Remember: if it's sprawling flat and growing in gravel or on concrete, it's likely Train Track Moss.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name suggesting it only grows on railroad tracks, this moss was actually growing on natural rock outcrops long before trains existed. The railroad environment just happens to mimic the harsh, well-drained conditions it evolved to love.
compareHints: Train Track Moss is the only species in its genus Drummondia found in New England, making it unique among our regional mosses. Compared to other members of the Orthotrichaceae family, it's distinguished by its creeping rather than cushion-forming growth habit and its preference for disturbed ground rather than tree bark or natural rock faces.
